script:
Interviewer: Welcome to our school careers programme. What made you interested in becoming an environmental engineer?
Layla: I enjoyed science, but I wanted to use it to solve practical problems in local communities.
Interviewer: Did you always know which job you wanted, or did your plans change during secondary school?
Layla: My plans changed several times. I considered teaching before joining a school project about water conservation.
Interviewer: What did the project involve, and which part of the work helped you most?
Layla: We measured water use, interviewed families and designed posters. I liked analysing results and suggesting improvements.
Interviewer: How did you find out what environmental engineers actually do during a normal working week?
Layla: Our teacher arranged an online conversation with a professional who explained field visits, reports and teamwork.
Interviewer: Did the engineer tell you that good examination results were the only requirement for success?
Layla: No. She emphasised communication, careful observation, problem solving and a willingness to learn from mistakes.
Interviewer: What advice did she give about choosing university subjects and planning future qualifications?
Layla: She suggested checking official entry requirements and speaking with advisers rather than relying on social-media rumours.
Interviewer: Some students feel pressure to choose a career immediately. What would you say to them?
Layla: Explore several possibilities. Talk to people who do different jobs and notice which tasks genuinely interest you.
Interviewer: Can short work-experience visits help, even if a student later chooses a completely different profession?
Layla: Certainly. A visit can reveal workplace routines and teach useful habits such as punctuality and respectful questions.
Interviewer: What was the biggest surprise when you visited a small engineering company during the holidays?
Layla: Engineers spent considerable time listening to clients and explaining choices, not just drawing technical plans.
Interviewer: How important is teamwork when people are working on complicated projects with limited budgets?
Layla: It is essential. Different specialists examine safety, costs and environmental effects before recommending a practical solution.
Interviewer: Have you ever made a mistake in a project, and what did you learn from it?
Layla: I once copied a measurement incorrectly. Our group checked the original notes and corrected the report together.
Interviewer: What are your next steps now that you have learned more about the field?
Layla: I will strengthen my mathematics, volunteer for another project and compare courses using official university information.
Interviewer: What final message would you give pupils who are still uncertain about their future careers?
Layla: Your first plan need not be permanent. Keep learning, ask thoughtful questions and choose opportunities that develop real skills.
